Confidence in God (verses 1–8)

Faith and prayer belong together. It is the prayer of faith that prevails.

David entrusted his soul to God in a particular way. Our Lord Jesus used the words of verse 5 when he gave up his last breath on the cross, offering himself willingly as a sacrifice for sin and laying down his life as a ransom.

David, however, spoke as a man in distress. His greatest concern was for his soul—his spirit and better part.

Some people think worldly business or multiplying worries excuse them from caring for their souls. In fact, troubles make such care even more urgent, so that the inner person need not suffer harm when the outward person wastes away.

The redemption of the soul is so precious that without Christ's undertaking, it would be lost forever.

Trusting divine mercy gives David reason to rejoice.

God observes whether suffering humbles us for sin and makes our souls better. His people will face dangers and rescues throughout life, until he finally delivers them from death, their last enemy.

Prayer amid distress (verses 9–18)

David's troubles made him a man of sorrows, picturing Christ, who was acquainted with grief.

There is an important difference: David recognized that his own sins deserved correction, while Christ suffered for our sins.

David's friends were too afraid to help him. We need not be surprised when human support fails, but we should make sure we have a Friend in heaven who never fails.

Those who place their spirits in God's hands can trust him to arrange everything for their ultimate good.

Our times are in God's hands: he may lengthen or shorten life and make its circumstances bitter or sweet according to his wise purposes.

Neither our own hands nor those of friends or enemies finally determine our course.

David therefore prayed to be saved for God's mercy, not because of personal merit.

He looked ahead to the day when those who slander and attack God's people will be silenced by divine judgment.

Meanwhile, let us seek to silence foolish accusations, if possible, by doing good.

Praise for God's goodness (verses 19–24)

Instead of giving way to despair or impatience, we should reflect upon how good God is to those who fear and trust him.

All mercy reaches sinners through the extraordinary gift of God's only Son as the atoning sacrifice.

Do not surrender to unbelief or assume that hardship means you have been cut off from God's sight and handed over to arrogant human enemies.

Lord, pardon our complaints and fears. Increase our faith, patience, love and gratitude. Teach us to rejoice in trouble and in hope.

Christ's deliverance and his victory over enemies should strengthen believers in every earthly affliction. Having suffered courageously with their Master, they will enter his joy and glory.

[Ps.31.1-Ps.31.8]
Chapter 31
Chapter Outline
Confidence in God. | (1-8) |
Prayer in trouble. | (9-18) |
Praise for God's goodness. | (19-24) |
Verses 1-8
Faith and prayer must go together, for the prayer of faith is the prevailing prayer. David gave up his soul in a special manner to God. And with the words, ver. 5, our Lord Jesus yielded up his last breath on the cross, and made his soul a free-will offering for sin, laying down his life as a ransom. But David is here as a man in distress and trouble. And his great care is about his soul, his spirit, his better part. Many think that while perplexed about their worldly affairs, and their cares multiply, they may be excused if they neglect their souls; but we are the more concerned to look to our souls, that, though the outward man perish, the inward man may suffer no damage. The redemption of the soul is so precious, that it must have ceased for ever, if Christ had not undertaken it. Having relied on God's mercy, he will be glad and rejoice in it. God looks upon our souls, when we are in trouble, to see whether they are humbled for sin, and made better by the affliction. Every believer will meet with such dangers and deliverances, until he is delivered from death, his last enemy.
[Ps.31.9-Ps.31.18]
Verses 9-18
David's troubles made him a man of sorrows. Herein he was a type of Christ, who was acquainted with grief. David acknowledged that his afflictions were merited by his own sins, but Christ suffered for ours. David's friends durst not give him any assistance. Let us not think it strange if thus deserted, but make sure of a Friend in heaven who will not fail. God will be sure to order and dispose all for the best, to all those who commit their spirits also into his hand. The time of life is in God's hands, to lengthen or shorten, make bitter or sweet, according to the counsel of his will. The way of man is not in himself, nor in our friend's hands, nor in our enemies' hands, but in God's. In this faith and confidence he prays that the Lord would save him for his mercies's sake, and not for any merit of his own. He prophesies the silencing of those that reproach and speak evil of the people of God. There is a day coming, when the Lord will execute judgment upon them. In the mean time, we should engage ourselves by well-doing, if possible, to silence the ignorance of foolish men.
[Ps.31.19-Ps.31.24]
Verses 19-24
Instead of yielding to impatience or despondency under our troubles, we should turn our thoughts to the goodness of the Lord towards those who fear and trust in Him. All comes to sinners through the wondrous gift of the only-begotten Son of God, to be the atonement for their sins. Let not any yield to unbelief, or think, under discouraging circumstances, that they are cut off from before the eyes of the Lord, and left to the pride of men. Lord, pardon our complaints and fears; increase our faith, patience, love, and gratitude; teach us to rejoice in tribulation and in hope. The deliverance of Christ, with the destruction of his enemies, ought to strengthen and comfort the hearts of believers under all their afflictions here below, that having suffered courageously with their Master, they may triumphantly enter into his joy and glory.

Happiness through forgiveness (verses 1 and 2)

Sin is the source of human misery. But the true believer's transgressions of God's law have been forgiven because they are covered by the atoning sacrifice.

Christ bore our sins; therefore God does not count them against us. Christ's righteousness is credited to us. God laid our sins upon him and made him a sin offering for us.

The decision not to count sin against someone belongs to God the Judge. It is God who justifies.

Yet the forgiven person is also sincere and seeks holiness through the Holy Spirit's power.

Such a person does not pretend to repent while intending to keep sinning because God is gracious. True believers do not misuse the doctrine of free grace as a license for sin.

God promises every kind of genuine blessing to those whose sins he forgives.

From the burden of sin to comfort (verses 3–7)

It is difficult to persuade sinners to receive free mercy humbly, confess their wrongdoing fully and condemn their own sin.

Yet confessing our sins before God is the only true path to peace of conscience.

Confession and repentance do not earn forgiveness, but are necessary to experience God's pardoning mercy.

How happy is the moment when a burdened soul is enabled to pour out its sorrow before God and embrace his covenant mercy in Christ Jesus!

We should seek the Lord when Providence calls us and his Spirit stirs us to turn toward him.

When guilt has softened the heart, every human refuge has failed and the troubled mind can find no rest, God applies the healing balm by his Spirit.

Instruction and encouragement (verses 8–11)

God teaches by his word and guides his people through his will.

The psalm warns sinners because the path of sin ends in sorrow.

It also comforts the saints: life in fellowship with God is truly the happiest and most satisfying life.

Lord Jesus, teach us to rejoice in you and in your salvation, so that our joy may be real.

[Ps.32.1-Ps.32.2]
Chapter 32
Chapter Outline
The happiness of a pardoned sinner. | (1-2) |
The misery that went before, and the comfort that followed the confession of sins. | (3-7) |
Sinners instructed, believers encouraged. | (8-11) |
Verses 1-2
Sin is the cause of our misery; but the true believer's transgressions of the Divine law are all forgiven, being covered with the atonement. Christ bare his sins, therefore they are not imputed to him. The righteousness of Christ being reckoned to us, and we being made the righteousness of God in him, our iniquity is not imputed, God having laid upon him the iniquity of us all, and made him a sin-offering for us. Not to impute sin, is God's act, for he is the Judge. It is God that justifies. Notice the character of him whose sins are pardoned; he is sincere, and seeks sanctification by the power of the Holy Ghost. He does not profess to repent, with an intention to indulge in sin, because the Lord is ready to forgive. He will not abuse the doctrine of free grace. And to the man whose iniquity is forgiven, all manner of blessings are promised.
[Ps.32.3-Ps.32.7]
Verses 3-7
It is very difficult to bring sinful man humbly to accept free mercy, with a full confession of his sins and self-condemnation. But the true and only way to peace of conscience, is, to confess our sins, that they may be forgiven; to declare them that we may be justified. Although repentance and confession do not merit the pardon of transgression, they are needful to the real enjoyment of forgiving mercy. And what tongue can tell the happiness of that hour, when the soul, oppressed by sin, is enabled freely to pour forth its sorrows before God, and to take hold of his covenanted mercy in Christ Jesus! Those that would speed in prayer, must seek the Lord, when, by his providence, he calls them to seek him, and, by his Spirit, stirs them up to seek him. In a time of finding, when the heart is softened with grief, and burdened with guilt; when all human refuge fails; when no rest can be found to the troubled mind, then it is that God applies the healing balm by his Spirit.
[Ps.32.8-Ps.32.11]
Verses 8-11
God teaches by his word, and guides with the secret intimations of his will. David gives a word of caution to sinners. The reason for this caution is, that the way of sin will certainly end in sorrow. Here is a word of comfort to saints. They may see that a life of communion with God is far the most pleasant and comfortable. Let us rejoice, O Lord Jesus, in thee, and in thy salvation; so shall we rejoice indeed.

God deserves our praise (verses 1–11)

Holy joy is at the heart of genuine praise. Thankful singing gives voice to that joy and is a fitting way to worship the Lord.

Every ability God has given us should be used with skill and earnestness in his service.

His promises are wise and good. His word is right, and we are right only insofar as we agree with it. Everything he does is done in truth.

Because the Lord is righteous, he loves righteousness.

How sad that an earth so full of signs of God's goodness should be so lacking in praise! Multitudes depend upon his generosity, yet so few live for his glory.

Whatever God does, he does effectively and permanently.

He overrules the plans of human beings and makes them serve his own purposes, even when the result surprises us. Nothing can prevent the fulfillment of his eternal counsel.

God's people trust his power (verses 12–22)

God knows every movement and intention of the human soul—even things hidden from all other people. He understands our hearts better than we do.

Our lives and hearts are in his hands; he formed the spirit of each person.

Every created power depends upon him. Without God it can accomplish nothing.

When we are secure in his favor, we need not fear what stands against us. Let us give him the glory for his particular grace.

Humanly devised methods to save our souls are useless. But the Lord's watchful eye rests on people who fear his name because they hope in his mercy.

He helps them in difficulty and preserves them from spiritual harm amid danger.

Whoever fears God and his judgment must also hope in his mercy. We cannot escape from him except by fleeing to him.

Lord, let your mercy be upon us. Give us its benefit and comfort—not according to what we deserve, but according to your promise and the faith your Spirit has created within us.

God to be praised. | (1-11) |

Holy joy is the heart and soul of praise, and that is here pressed upon the righteous. Thankful praise is the breath and language of holy joy. All the motions and operations of the souls of men, which no mortals know but themselves, God knows better than they do. Their hearts, as well as their times, are all in his hand; he formed the spirit of each man within him. All the powers of the creature depend upon him, and are of no account, of no avail at all, without him. If we make God's favour sure towards us, then we need not fear whatever is against us. We are to give to him the glory of his special grace. All human devices for the salvation of our souls are vain; but the Lord's watchful eye is over those whose conscientious fear of his name proceeds from a believing hope in his mercy. In difficulties they shall be helped; in dangers they shall not receive any real damage. Those that fear God and his wrath, must hope in God and his mercy; for there is no flying from him, but by flying to him. Let thy mercy, O Lord, be upon us; let us always have the comfort and benefit, not according to our merits, but according to the promise which thou hast in thy word given to us, and according to the faith thou hast by thy Spirit and grace wrought in us.

David praises God and invites others to trust (verses 1–10)

If we hope to spend eternity praising God, we should devote much of this life to praising him.

He has never told anyone to seek him without hope of an answer.

David's prayers helped overcome his fears. Many others have looked to God through faith and prayer and found renewed courage and comfort.

Looking to the world leaves us perplexed and uncertain. Looking to Christ is essential to our salvation and every blessing that belongs to it.

The poor person whom society neither respects nor notices can still approach the throne of grace. The Lord hears and delivers.

Holy angels minister to the saints and defend them against powers of darkness. Yet all glory belongs to the Lord of the angels, not to his servants.

Taste and sight allow us both to discover and to enjoy. Taste and see that the Lord is good: recognize his kindness and take comfort in it.

Whoever truly trusts him is blessed.

For the coming life, God's people receive grace sufficient to sustain them spiritually. For this life, they receive what is genuinely necessary from him.

Paul could say he possessed everything and abounded because he had learned contentment (Philippians 4:11–18).

Those who trust only their own strength and efforts will eventually find themselves lacking. Those who rely on the Lord and quietly carry out their responsibilities will be cared for.

Learn the fear of the Lord (verses 11–22)

Young people should begin life by learning to fear the Lord. Those who start early in his service enjoy a greater opportunity for comfort now and happiness forever.

Everyone wants to be happy. But human life is short and troubled, so genuine happiness must reach beyond this world.

The way of faith requires watchfulness over heart and tongue.

Not harming others is not enough: we must strive to be useful and do good.

We should seek peace and pursue it, willingly giving up some personal advantage for its sake.

When genuine believers suffer, they habitually call upon God and are comforted that he hears them.

The righteous are humble about their sins and do not think highly of themselves.

Nothing is more necessary for true godliness than a contrite heart free from self-confidence. Grace flourishes in such soil, and the free, rich gospel of Jesus Christ is its encouragement.

The Lord specially protects righteous people, yet they still experience many trials and hatred from others. Divine mercy itself may correct them, and the enemy of their souls also attacks them.

But their troubles cannot ultimately destroy their souls, because the Lord keeps them from falling into sin during suffering.

No one is truly desolate except the person whom God has abandoned.

Verses 1-10
If we hope to spend eternity in praising God, it is fit that we should spend much of our time here in this work. He never said to any one, Seek ye me in vain. David's prayers helped to silence his fears; many besides him have looked unto the Lord by faith and prayer, and it has wonderfully revived and comforted them. When we look to the world, we are perplexed, and at a loss. But on looking to Christ depends our whole salvation, and all things needful thereunto do so also. This poor man, whom no man looked upon with any respect, or looked after with any concern, was yet welcome to the throne of grace; the Lord heard him, and saved him out of all his troubles. The holy angels minister to the saints, and stand for them against the powers of darkness. All the glory be to the Lord of the angels. By taste and sight we both make discoveries, and have enjoyment; Taste and see God's goodness; take notice of it, and take the comfort of it. He makes all truly blessed that trust in him. As to the things of the other world, they shall have grace sufficient for the support of spiritual life. And as to this life, they shall have what is necessary from the hand of God. Paul had all, and abounded, because he was content, [Phil.4.11-Phil.4.18] Php 4:11-18. Those who trust to themselves, and think their own efforts sufficient for them, shall want; but they shall be fed who trust in the Lord. Those shall not want, who with quietness work, and mind their own business.
[Ps.34.11-Ps.34.22]
Verses 11-22
Let young persons set out in life with learning the fear of the Lord, if they desire true comfort here, and eternal happiness hereafter. Those will be most happy who begin the soonest to serve so good a Master. All aim to be happy. Surely this must look further than the present world; for man's life on earth consists but of few days, and those full of trouble. What man is he that would see the good of that where all bliss is perfect? Alas! few have this good in their thoughts. That religion promises best which creates watchfulness over the heart and over the tongue. It is not enough not to do hurt, we must study to be useful, and to live to some purpose; we must seek peace and pursue it; be willing to deny ourselves a great deal for peace' sake. It is the constant practice of real believers, when in distress, to cry unto God, and it is their constant comfort that he hears them. The righteous are humbled for sin, and are low in their own eyes. Nothing is more needful to true godliness than a contrite heart, broken off from every self-confidence. In this soil every grace will flourish, and nothing can encourage such a one but the free, rich grace of the gospel of Jesus Christ. The righteous are taken under the special protection of the Lord, yet they have their share of crosses in this world, and there are those that hate them. Both from the mercy of Heaven, and the malice of hell, the afflictions of the righteous must be many. But whatever troubles befal them, shall not hurt their souls, for God keeps them from sinning in troubles. No man is desolate, but he whom God has forsaken.

David prays for protection (verses 1–10)

It is no surprise for righteous people or righteous causes to have enemies. The hostility of the serpent's offspring against the woman's Seed has been present since the beginning.

David in affliction, Christ in suffering, the persecuted church and the tempted Christian all look to Almighty God to defend their cause.

We often justify anxiety and anger over unjust treatment by saying we gave others no reason to mistreat us.

Yet our innocence should actually bring comfort: we may more confidently entrust the case to the Lord.

David asked God to make his presence known in the trial and to grant inward consolation amid outward distress.

If God's Spirit assures us inwardly that he is our salvation, we need nothing else to make us truly happy.

If God is our Friend, it does not matter who opposes us.

Henry understands David's words against his enemies as prophetic announcements of just divine judgment, anticipating the fate of Christ's enemies.

He adds an essential distinction: Christians must not desire or pray for the destruction of human opponents. The enemies whose ruin we should seek are our sinful desires and the evil spirits that seek our destruction.

A traveler caught at night on a slippery, dangerous road pictures the sinner moving through temptation.

Having entrusted his cause to the Lord, David expected deliverance and pledged to praise God with all his strength.

Such language is even more fitting when applied to heavenly rescue in Christ.

David describes the ingratitude of enemies (verses 11–16)

Few accusations are worse than that someone has repaid kindness with cruelty.

That was the character of David's enemies. In this experience he pictured Christ.

David had shown genuine tenderness while his enemies suffered.

We should grieve over the sins of people who do not grieve for themselves.

Doing good to the ungrateful is never ultimately wasted.

Let us learn patience and gentleness from David—and still more from Christ's example.

David asks God to rescue his soul (verses 17–28)

God's people seek peaceful lives, yet their enemies often devise false accusations and plots against them.

David prayed: My soul is in danger. Lord, rescue it. It belongs to you, the Father of spirits; claim and save what is yours. Do not stand far off as though I were a stranger.

The One who exalted the once-suffering Redeemer will also defend his people.

The roaring lion will not destroy their souls, any more than he could destroy Christ, their Surety.

Believers entrust their souls to God's hands. Through faith they are united with Christ, precious in God's sight and assured of deliverance from ultimate destruction.

Their rescue will lead them to give thanks in heaven.

[Ps.35.1-Ps.35.10]
Chapter 35
Chapter Outline
David prays for safety. | (1-10) |
He complains of his enemies. | (11-16) |
And calls upon God to support him. | (17-28) |
Verses 1-10
It is no new thing for the most righteous men, and the most righteous cause, to meet with enemies. This is a fruit of the old enmity in the seed of the serpent against the Seed of the woman. David in his afflictions, Christ in his sufferings, the church under persecution, and the Christian in the hour temptation, all beseech the Almighty to appear in their behalf, and to vindicate their cause. We are apt to justify uneasiness at the injuries men do us, by our never having given them cause to use us so ill; but this should make us easy, for then we may the more expect that God will plead our cause. David prayed to God to manifest himself in his trial. Let me have inward comfort under all outward troubles, to support my soul. If God, by his Spirit, witness to our spirits that he is our salvation, we need desire no more to make us happy. If God is our Friend, no matter who is our enemy. By the Spirit of prophecy, David foretells the just judgments of God that would come upon his enemies for their great wickedness. These are predictions, they look forward, and show the doom of the enemies of Christ and his kingdom. We must not desire or pray for the ruin of any enemies, except our lusts and the evil spirits that would compass our destruction. A traveller benighted in a bad road, is an expressive emblem of a sinner walking in the slippery and dangerous ways of temptation. But David having committed his cause to God, did not doubt of his own deliverance. The bones are the strongest parts of the body. The psalmist here proposes to serve and glorify God with all his strength. If such language may be applied to outward salvation, how much more will it apply to heavenly things in Christ Jesus!
[Ps.35.11-Ps.35.16]
Verses 11-16
Call a man ungrateful, and you can call him no worse: this was the character of David's enemies. Herein he was a type of Christ. David shows how tenderly he had behaved towards them in afflictions. We ought to mourn for the sins of those who do not mourn for themselves. We shall not lose by the good offices we do to any, how ungrateful soever they may be. Let us learn to possess our souls in patience and meekness like David, or rather after Christ's example.
[Ps.35.17-Ps.35.28]
Verses 17-28
Though the people of God are, and study to be, quiet, yet it has been common for their enemies to devise deceitful matters against them. David prays, My soul is in danger, Lord, rescue it; it belongs to thee the Father of spirits, therefore claim thine own; it is thine, save it! Lord, be not far from me, as if I were a stranger. He who exalted the once suffering Redeemer, will appear for all his people: the roaring lion shall not destroy their souls, any more than he could that of Christ, their Surety. They trust their souls in his hands, they are one with him by faith, are precious in his sight, and shall be rescued from destruction, that they may give thanks in heaven.

The condition of wicked people (verses 1–4)

This psalm should deepen our hatred of sin and our desire for God's loving-kindness.

The root of wickedness is contempt for God and the refusal to show him proper reverence. Another root is self-deception.

We should ask God every day to protect us from flattering ourselves.

Sin does terrible harm to the person practicing it, and for that reason should be hated. Yet sinners too easily regard it as harmless.

If people deceive themselves, it is not surprising when they deceive others. A person false to their own soul can scarcely be trusted by anybody.

It is wrong to do evil; it is worse to plan evil deliberately, organizing it with care.

When we willingly drive holy thoughts from our minds during quiet hours, Satan is ready to replace them with sinful imaginings.

Hardened sinners become so stubborn that they defend their actions as though they could justify them before God himself.

The goodness of God (verses 5–12)

Human beings may refuse compassion, but God's mercy remains available. That is great comfort to believers.

God acts wisely and well. We do not now understand everything he does, but we will know enough at the proper time.

His loving-kindness is precious to those who trust him. They place themselves beneath his protection and find security and peace.

A gracious person always wants more of God, but never wants anything greater than God.

God's providential gifts allow believers to be content with what they possess.

His appointed ordinances are sweet and strengthen spiritual life, yet complete satisfaction is reserved for the world to come.

God prepares his people to desire those pleasures and fills them by his Spirit with joy and peace in believing.

He gives life to whom he wills. Whoever is willing may come and take freely from the water of life.

May we know, love and sincerely serve the Lord. Then no proud enemy on earth or power from hell can separate us from his love.

Faith looks ahead as though the promised things had already occurred. It shows us the Lord upon his throne of judgment and the dominion of sin overthrown forever.
classic_reading:
[Ps.36.1-Ps.36.4]
Chapter 36
Chapter Outline
The bad state of the wicked. | (1-4) |
The goodness of God. | (5-12) |
Verses 1-4
From this psalm our hearts should be duly affected with hatred of sin, and seek satisfaction in God's loving-kindness. Here is the root of bitterness, from which all the wickedness of wicked men comes. It takes rise from contempt of God, and the want of due regard to him. Also from the deceit they put upon their own souls. Let us daily beg of God to preserve us from self-flattery. Sin is very hurtful to the sinner himself, and therefore ought to be hateful; but it is not so. It is no marvel, if those that deceive themselves, seek to deceive all mankind; to whom will they be true, who are false to their own souls? It is bad to do mischief, but worse to devise it, to do it with plot and management. If we willingly banish holy meditations in our solitary hours, Satan will soon occupy our minds with sinful imaginations. Hardened sinners stand to what they have done, as though they could justify it before God himself.
[Ps.36.5-Ps.36.12]
Verses 5-12
Men may shut up their compassion, yet, with God we shall find mercy. This is great comfort to all believers, plainly to be seen, and not to be taken away. God does all wisely and well; but what he does we know not now, it is time enough to know hereafter. God's loving-kindness is precious to the saints. They put themselves under his protection, and then are safe and easy. Gracious souls, though still desiring more of God, never desire more than God. The gifts of Providence so far satisfy them, that they are content with such things as they have. The benefit of holy ordinances is sweet to a sanctified soul, and strengthening to the spiritual and Divine life. But full satisfaction is reserved for the future state. Their joys shall be constant. God not only works in them a gracious desire for these pleasures, but by his Spirit fills their souls with joy and peace in believing. He quickens whom he will; and whoever will, may come, and take from him of the waters of life freely. May we know, and love, and uprightly serve the Lord; then no proud enemy, on earth or from hell, shall separate us from his love. Faith calleth things that are not, as though they were. It carries us forward to the end of time; it shows us the Lord, on his throne of judgment; the empire of sin fallen to rise no more.

Original heading

David persuades to patience and confidence in God, by the state of the godly and of the wicked.

Original source divisionsSource commentaryVersesFirst section1–6Second section7–20Third section21–33Fourth section34–40
Do not envy the wicked (verses 1–6)

The world contains many wicked people who prosper and live in comfort. That was true in David's day and should not surprise us now.

Their success tempts us to be resentful, to mistake them for the happiest people and eventually to imitate them.

But outward prosperity fades. Those who look forward with faith see no reason to envy wicked people, whose judgment is everlasting.

True religion is trust in the Lord expressed through diligent obedience. To claim trust while neglecting duty is to test God, not trust him.

Life does not consist in possessions. Enough food and provision for our needs is more than we deserve and sufficient for someone traveling toward heaven.

Delighting in God is both a duty and a privilege.

He has not promised to gratify every bodily appetite or whim, but to satisfy the desires of a soul renewed and made holy.

The true desire of a godly heart is to know, love and serve God.

To commit our way to the Lord is to roll its burden upon him: bring our concerns before him in prayer and avoid tormenting ourselves about future events.

We must do our duty and leave what happens afterward in his hands.

Wait patiently for the Lord (verses 7–20)

Trust that God will make everything work for our ultimate good. Do not become agitated by what you see in this world, because a discontented spirit invites many temptations.

The little given to a righteous person is better and more useful than abundant wealth acquired or used wickedly. It comes from the hand of special divine love.

God provides for his servants both when they work and when they wait.

They possess something better than worldly wealth: peace of conscience, peace with God and peace in God—peace the world cannot give.

God knows all the days of his people, and not one day's faithful work will go unrewarded.

Earthly days are quickly numbered, but heavenly happiness endures forever.

Those resting upon the Rock of Ages need not envy wicked people leaning upon broken reeds.

Righteousness, generosity and divine guidance (verses 21–33)

God requires us to act justly and give others what is owed.

It is a serious sin to refuse payment of a just debt when able to pay; it is a serious hardship to be unable to pay.

Truly merciful people continue showing mercy. We must abandon sin, learn to do good and persist in doing so.

God's blessing is the source, sweetness and security of every earthly comfort. Those assured of his favor will lack nothing truly good for them.

By grace and the Holy Spirit, he directs the thoughts, affections and plans of his people; by Providence he orders events to guide them.

He does not always show the whole road. He often leads one step at a time, as a parent guides a child.

A believer may fall into sin or trouble, and the sin may bring real pain. But God will keep such a person from ultimate ruin.

Few, if any, have seen a consistent believer and all that believer's children left in complete, friendless destitution.

God does not abandon his saints in affliction. Their permanent home, however, is heaven.

Even when Satan buffets a faithful person severely, God does not leave that person in the enemy's hands.

Trust the Lord for the outcome (verses 34–40)

Duty belongs to us; outcomes belong to God.

Verses 35 and 36 picture the apparently flourishing enemy of God whose prosperity soon disappears.

The Lord brings proud plans to nothing, especially plans of persecutors.

No one is perfect in personal righteousness; believers are made complete in Christ Jesus.

Even if a believer's whole life seems dark and cloudy, the final days may be peaceful. And if death itself comes under a cloud, eternal peace still awaits.

Salvation belongs to the Lord. He helps his people fulfill their duties, bear their burdens, endure difficulties profitably and, in his time, escape them.

Let sinners therefore turn from evil and do good. Let them repent, abandon sin and trust God's mercy through Jesus Christ.

Let them take Christ's yoke and learn from him, so that they may dwell in heaven forever.

Consider the different endings of human lives, and always depend on God's mercy.
classic_reading:
[Ps.37.1-Ps.37.6]
Chapter 37
David persuades to patience and confidence in God, by the state of the godly and of the wicked.
Verses 1-6
When we look abroad we see the world full of evil-doers, that flourish and live in ease. So it was seen of old, therefore let us not marvel at the matter. We are tempted to fret at this, to think them the only happy people, and so we are prone to do like them: but this we are warned against. Outward prosperity is fading. When we look forward, with an eye of faith, we shall see no reason to envy the wicked. Their weeping and wailing will be everlasting. The life of religion is a believing trust in the Lord, and diligent care to serve him according to his will. It is not trusting God, but tempting him, if we do not make conscience of our duty to him. A man's life consists not in abundance, but, Thou shalt have food convenient for thee. This is more than we deserve, and it is enough for one that is going to heaven. To delight in God is as much a privilege as a duty. He has not promised to gratify the appetites of the body, and the humours of the fancy, but the desires of the renewed, sanctified soul. What is the desire of the heart of a good man? It is this, to know, and love, and serve God. Commit thy way unto the Lord; roll thy way upon the Lord, so the margin reads it. Cast thy burden upon the Lord, the burden of thy care. We must roll it off ourselves, not afflict and perplex ourselves with thoughts about future events, but refer them to God. By prayer spread thy case and all thy cares before the Lord, and trust in him. We must do our duty, and then leave the event with God. The promise is very sweet: He shall bring that to pass, whatever it is, which thou has committed to him.
[Ps.37.7-Ps.37.20]
Verses 7-20
Let us be satisfied that God will make all to work for good to us. Let us not discompose ourselves at what we see in this world. A fretful, discontented spirit is open to many temptations. For, in all respects, the little which is allotted to the righteous, is more comfortable and more profitable than the ill-gotten and abused riches of ungodly men. It comes from a hand of special love. God provides plentifully and well, not only for his working servants, but for his waiting servants. They have that which is better than wealth, peace of mind, peace with God, and then peace in God; that peace which the world cannot give, and which the world cannot have. God knows the believer's days. Not one day's work shall go unrewarded. Their time on earth is reckoned by days, which will soon be numbered; but heavenly happiness shall be for ever. This will be a real support to believers in evil times. Those that rest on the Rock of ages, have no reason to envy the wicked the support of their broken reeds.
[Ps.37.21-Ps.37.33]
Verses 21-33
The Lord our God requires that we do justly, and render to all their due. It is a great sin for those that are able, to deny the payment of just debts; it is a great misery not to be able to pay them. He that is truly merciful, will be ever merciful. We must leave our sins; learn to do well, and cleave to it. This is true religion. The blessing of God is the spring, sweetness, and security of all earthly enjoyments. And if we are sure of this, we are sure not to want any thing good for us in this world. By his grace and Holy Spirit, he directs the thoughts, affections, and designs of good men. By his providence he overrules events, so as to make their way plain. He does not always show them his way for a distance, but leads them step by step, as children are led. God will keep them from being ruined by their falls, either into sin or into trouble, though such as fall into sin will be sorely hurt. Few, if any, have known the consistent believer, or his children, reduced to abject, friendless want. God forsakes not his saints in affliction; and in heaven only the righteous shall dwell for ever; that will be their everlasting habitation. A good man may fall into the hands of a messenger of Satan, and be sorely buffeted, but God will not leave him in his enemy's hands.
[Ps.37.34-Ps.37.40]
Verses 34-40
Duty is ours, and we must mind it; but events are God's, we must refer the disposal of them to him. What a striking picture is in ver. #(35-36), of many a prosperous enemy of God! But God remarkably blights the projects of the prosperous wicked, especially persecutors. None are perfect in themselves, but believers are so in Christ Jesus. If all the saint's days continue dark and cloudy, his dying day may prove comfortable, and his sun set bright; or, if it should set under a cloud, yet his future state will be everlasting peace. The salvation of the righteous will be the Lord's doing. He will help them to do their duties, to bear their burdens; help them to bear their troubles well, and get good by them, and, in due time, will deliver them out of their troubles. Let sinners then depart from evil, and do good; repent of and forsake sin, and trust in the mercy of God through Jesus Christ. Let them take his yoke upon them, and learn of him, that they may dwell for evermore in heaven. Let us mark the closing scenes of different characters, and always depend on God's mercy.

The burden of sin (verses 1–11)

Nothing troubles a godly heart as much as the feeling that God is angry.

We remain at peace by keeping ourselves in his love.

Yet the guilt of sin is too heavy for any person to bear. Without God's pardoning mercy, it leads to despair and destruction.

Henry sees human sickness and pain as effects of sin's entrance into creation: without sin there would be no suffering in the body. The whole creation groans beneath the burden of guilt and corruption.

That burden falls upon sinners either as sorrow drawing them to seek mercy or as final destruction if they remain unrepentant.

When we understand our condition, we will value and seek the Good Physician.

Many allow their spiritual wounds to worsen because they delay going to their merciful Friend.

During bodily illness, we should remember how our bodies have dishonored God and ask him to teach us repentance.

Even groanings too deep for words are known to the One who searches hearts and knows the Spirit's mind.

David's suffering also pictured Christ in his agony and upon his cross, suffering amid abandonment.

Suffering, patience and prayer (verses 12–22)

Wicked people may hate goodness even while benefiting from it.

In his descriptions of hostile enemies, David again points toward Christ.

Other people can do us lasting harm only if they persuade us to abandon God and neglect duty.

The true believer's distress can become useful through learning to wait upon God rather than looking only to the world or personal power for relief.

Often our minds will be quieter when we pay less attention to the insults and injuries others inflict.

David suffered correction for his own transgressions, but Christ suffered for our sins alone.

Why should sinners respond with anger or impatience when God mercifully corrects them?

David was aware of sinful impulses still working within him.

When good people continually look only at their suffering, they may lose their balance; when they keep God before them, they remain standing.

True repentance makes us patient during correction.

For a suffering believer, nothing is more painful than the fear of being abandoned by God.

Therefore the heartfelt prayer is: “Do not be far from me.”

The Lord will come to help those who trust him as their salvation.

Chapter 38
Chapter Outline
God's displeasure at sin. | (1-11) |
The psalmist's sufferings and prayers. | (12-22) |
Verses 1-11
Nothing will disquiet the heart of a good man so much as the sense of God's anger. The way to keep the heart quiet, is to keep ourselves in the love of God. But a sense of guilt is too heavy to bear; and would sink men into despair and ruin, unless removed by the pardoning mercy of God. If there were not sin in our souls, there would be no pain in our bones, no illness in our bodies. The guilt of sin is a burden to the whole creation, which groans under it. It will be a burden to the sinners themselves, when they are heavy-laden under it, or a burden of ruin, when it sinks them to hell. When we perceive our true condition, the Good Physician will be valued, sought, and obeyed. Yet many let their wounds rankle, because they delay to go to their merciful Friend. When, at any time, we are distempered in our bodies, we ought to remember how God has been dishonoured in and by our bodies. The groanings which cannot be uttered, are not hid from Him that searches the heart, and knows the mind of the Spirit. David, in his troubles, was a type of Christ in his agonies, of Christ on his cross, suffering and deserted.
[Ps.38.12-Ps.38.22]
Verses 12-22
Wicked men hate goodness, even when they benefit by it. David, in the complaints he makes of his enemies, seems to refer to Christ. But our enemies do us real mischief only when they drive us from God and our duty. The true believer's trouble will be made useful; he will learn to wait for his God, and will not seek relief from the world or himself. The less we notice the unkindness and injuries that are done us, the more we consult the quiet of our own minds. David's troubles were the chastisement and the consequence of his transgressions, whilst Christ suffered for our sins and ours only. What right can a sinner have to yield to impatience or anger, when mercifully corrected for his sins? David was very sensible of the present workings of corruption in him. Good men, by setting their sorrow continually before them, have been ready to fall; but by setting God always before them, they have kept their standing. If we are truly penitent for sin, that will make us patient under affliction. Nothing goes nearer to the heart of a believer when in affliction, than to be under the apprehension of God's deserting him; nor does any thing come more feelingly from his heart than this prayer, "Be not far from me." The Lord will hasten to help those who trust in him as their salvation.

Guarding speech and remembering mortality (verses 1–6)

When an evil thought arises, we should suppress it.

Habitual watchfulness is the bridle on the horse's head; watchfulness in particular moments is the hand holding the bridle.

When we cannot avoid the company of wicked people, we should remember that they watch our words and may twist them to injure us.

Sometimes silence is necessary, even when what we could say is good. But generally we do wrong if we continually avoid opportunities for speech that would help others.

Impatience begins within us, often through brooding thoughts. Its outward consequence is a burning agitation of the soul.

Even in excellent health and prosperity, every person is fragile and passing away. No one can live long by earthly standards, and death may arrive very soon.

This is certain, yet we are reluctant to accept it.

Let us ask God to enlighten our minds by his Holy Spirit and fill our hearts with grace, so that we are prepared to die at any day or hour.

Pardon, deliverance and hope (verses 7–13)

Created things cannot provide lasting satisfaction.

We find it only in the Lord and fellowship with him; disappointments should bring us back to that truth.

If the world is empty and passing, may God prevent us from seeking our ultimate portion in it.

When confidence in created things fails, we still have God to whom we can turn and in whom we can trust.

Recognizing that a good God orders our affairs helps us accept his discipline without accusing him.

David sought forgiveness and asked to be protected from shame.

We must watch and pray against sin. When God corrects us, we should seek relief from him, not put our confidence elsewhere.

Our own conduct often brings trouble, as though we are struck by a rod we made ourselves.

Human beauty is a poor foundation for pride. It will certainly fade, perhaps very quickly.

The body is like a garment worn by the soul. Sin has introduced a moth into that garment, wearing away its beauty, then its strength, and finally its very substance.

Watching a slow disease or the progress of age makes this image painfully clear.

Suffering can stir us to prayer. If it does, we have reason to hope God will hear us.

Believers may expect weariness and poor treatment while traveling toward heaven, but their journey here is short.

Walking by faith, they can continue without abandoning their course or collapsing under hardships.

How blessed it is to hold earthly things loosely as we go home to our Father's house, using the world without misusing it.

Let us look toward the city whose Builder and Maker is God.

[Ps.39.1-Ps.39.6]
Chapter 39
Chapter Outline
David meditates on man's frailty. | (1-6) |
He applies for pardon and deliverance. | (7-13) |
Verses 1-6
If an evil thought should arise in the mind, suppress it. Watchfulness in the habit, is the bridle upon the head; watchfulness in acts, is the hand upon the bridle. When not able to separate from wicked men, we should remember they will watch our words, and turn them, if they can, to our disadvantage. Sometimes it may be necessary to keep silence, even from good words; but in general we are wrong when backward to engage in edifying discourse. Impatience is a sin that has its cause within ourselves, and that is, musing; and its ill effects upon ourselves, and that is no less than burning. In our greatest health and prosperity, every man is altogether vanity, he cannot live long; he may die soon. This is an undoubted truth, but we are very unwilling to believe it. Therefore let us pray that God would enlighten our minds by his Holy Spirit, and fill our hearts with his grace, that we may be ready for death every day and hour.
[Ps.39.7-Ps.39.13]
Verses 7-13
There is no solid satisfaction to be had in the creature; but it is to be found in the Lord, and in communion with him; to him we should be driven by our disappointments. If the world be nothing but vanity, may God deliver us from having or seeking our portion in it. When creature-confidences fail, it is our comfort that we have a God to go to, a God to trust in. We may see a good God doing all, and ordering all events concerning us; and a good man, for that reason, says nothing against it. He desires the pardoning of his sin, and the preventing of his shame. We must both watch and pray against sin. When under the correcting hand of the Lord, we must look to God himself for relief, not to any other. Our ways and our doings bring us into trouble, and we are beaten with a rod of our own making. What a poor thing is beauty! and what fools are those that are proud of it, when it will certainly, and may quickly, be consumed! The body of man is as a garment to the soul. In this garment sin has lodged a moth, which wears away, first the beauty, then the strength, and finally the substance of its parts. Whoever has watched the progress of a lingering distemper, or the work of time alone, in the human frame, will feel at once the force of this comparison, and that, surely every man is vanity. Afflictions are sent to stir up prayer. If they have that effect, we may hope that God will hear our prayer. The believer expects weariness and ill treatment on his way to heaven; but he shall not stay here long : walking with God by faith, he goes forward on his journey, not diverted from his course, nor cast down by the difficulties he meets. How blessed it is to sit loose from things here below, that while going home to our Father's house, we may use the world as not abusing it! May we always look for that city, whose Builder and Maker is God.

Deliverance after patient waiting (verses 1–5)

Fears and doubts about our eternal state can feel like a dreadful pit full of sticky mud, even to a dearly loved child of God.

Yet the Lord has enough power to help the weakest and enough grace to help the most unworthy person who trusts him.

The psalmist waited patiently, continuing to believe, hope and pray.

Henry sees these words as applying especially to Christ, whose agony in Gethsemane and on the cross resembled that dreadful pit.

Those who wait for God will never wait in vain.

Believers who have suffered spiritual despair and then found relief by God's grace recognize themselves in verse 2.

Christ is the Rock on which a struggling soul can stand securely.

Where God grants firm hope, he also expects a steady and orderly life.

David received not only peace through faith but also joy.

Multitudes have looked in faith to Christ's suffering and glory and learned both to fear God's justice and to trust his mercy.

God loads us daily with benefits through Providence and grace.

The work of redemption (verses 6–10)

Here David foretold the wonder of redemption through Jesus Christ.

The true substance had to appear. Animal sacrifices could never give God the glory or human beings the saving grace accomplished by Christ.

The psalm speaks of Jesus being set apart to serve as Mediator.

The scroll of the book spoke of him.

Henry also sees the covenant of redemption as recorded in God's eternal counsel, and points to the Old Testament's testimony about Christ (John 19:28).

Now that the price of salvation has been paid, its proclamation goes out, inviting people freely and openly to receive it.

Preaching Christ is not easy. People commissioned to proclaim the gospel may face pressure to hide its truth, but Christ sustains those he calls.

May we believe his testimony, trust his promises and submit to his authority.

Seeking mercy and grace (verses 11–17)

Even the best saints know they would be undone without God's continuing protection and grace.

See how seriously David regarded sin. This makes the discovery of a Redeemer especially welcome.

When he examined each part of his life, he found something wrong.

A clear view of our sins without an equally clear view of the Savior would overwhelm us.

Yet Christ has triumphed over our spiritual enemies, and through him we are more than conquerors.

Let everyone who seeks God and loves his salvation rejoice and praise him.

No poverty or sorrow can make a person who fears the Lord truly miserable. God himself, together with all he has done and promised, is the source of that person's joy.

The prayer of faith draws upon his inexhaustible fullness, sufficient for every need.

His promises are certain and their fulfillment approaches.

The One who first came in humility will return in glorious majesty.

Verses 1-5
Doubts and fears about the eternal state, are a horrible pit and miry clay, and have been so to many a dear child of God. There is power enough in God to help the weakest, and grace enough to help the unworthiest of all that trust in him. The psalmist waited patiently; he continued believing, hoping, and praying. This is applicable to Christ. His agony, in the garden and on the cross, was a horrible pit and miry clay. But those that wait patiently for God do not wait in vain. Those that have been under religious melancholy, and by the grace of God have been relieved, may apply ver. #(2) very feelingly to themselves; they are brought up out of a horrible pit. Christ is the Rock on which a poor soul can alone stand fast. Where God has given stedfast hope, he expects there should be a steady, regular walk and conduct. God filled the psalmist with joy, as well as peace in believing. Multitudes, by faith beholding the sufferings and glory of Christ, have learned to fear the justice and trust in the mercy of God through Him. Many are the benefits with which we are daily loaded, both by the providence and by the grace of God.
[Ps.40.6-Ps.40.10]
Verses 6-10
The psalmist foretells that work of wonder, redemption by our Lord Jesus Christ. The Substance must come, which is Christ, who must bring that glory to God, and that grace to man, which it was impossible the sacrifices should ever do. Observe the setting apart of our Lord Jesus to the work and office of Mediator. In the volume, or roll, of the book it was written of him. In the close rolls of the Divine decrees and counsel, the covenant of redemption was recorded. Also, in all the volumes of the Old Testament something was written of him, [John.19.28] Joh 19:28. Now the purchase of our salvation is made, the proclamation is sent forth, calling us to come and accept it. It was preached freely and openly. Whoever undertook to preach the gospel of Christ, would be under great temptation to conceal it; but Christ, and those he calls to that work, are carried on in it. May we believe his testimony, trust his promise, and submit to his authority.
[Ps.40.11-Ps.40.17]
Verses 11-17
The best saints see themselves undone, unless continually preserved by the grace of God. But see the frightful view the psalmist had of sin. This made the discovery of a Redeemer so welcome. In all his reflections upon each step of his life, he discovered something amiss. The sight and sense of our sins in their own colours, must distract us, if we have not at the same time some sight of a Saviour. If Christ has triumphed over our spiritual enemies, then we, through him, shall be more than conquerors. This may encourage all that seek God and love his salvation, to rejoice in him, and to praise him. No griefs nor poverty can render those miserable who fear the Lord. Their God, and all that he has or does, is the ground of their joy. The prayer of faith can unlock his fulness, which is adapted to all their wants. The promises are sure, the moment of fulfilment hastens forward. He who once came in great humility, shall come again in glorious majesty.
